proposals.after: The empress's father Ye was posthumously granted the office of Senior Grand Master of the Palace with the Golden Seal and Purple Cord.

proposals.before: When the crown prince's position was fixed, the authorities memorialized: "The crown prince stands second to the throne, and all the realm performs official rites. Having paid full ritual to the heir, one cannot withhold respect from his mother. Princesses who may exchange correspondence, and the three ladies of the six palaces who share the honored consort's rank, should all observe toward her the same rites owed the crown prince. In the Yuanjia era of Song, retainers of Shixing and Wuling paid official respect to their princes' mothers, Consorts Pan and Lu. Though the honored consort is not the lesser lord to palace officials, the principle matches the Taizong reign of Song, when officials were ordered to pay official respect to the emperor's mother. Palace staff should show respect as officials do, presenting memorials at the Divine Beast Gate and offering year-end congratulations in the same way. Moreover, the crown prince's consort is paired by grand precedent; for a daughter-in-law to outrank her mother-in-law would violate order. The honored consort's regulations should match the crown prince's in full."
proposals.after: When the crown prince's position was fixed, the authorities memorialized: "The crown prince stands second to the throne, and all the realm performs official rites. Having paid full ritual to the heir, one cannot withhold respect from his mother. Princesses who may exchange correspondence, and the three ladies of the six palaces who share the honored consort's rank, should all observe toward her the same rites owed the crown prince. In the Yuanjia era of Song, retainers of Shixing and Wuling paid official respect to their princes' mothers, Consorts Pan and Lu. Though the honored consort is not the lesser lord to palace officials, the principle matches the Taiyu reign of Song, when officials were ordered to pay official respect to the emperor's mother. Palace staff should show respect as officials do, presenting memorials at the Divine Beast Gate and offering year-end congratulations in the same way. Moreover, the crown prince's consort is paired by grand precedent; for a daughter-in-law to outrank her mother-in-law would violate order. The honored consort's regulations should match the crown prince's in full."
proposals.reason: Chinese 泰豫 is the Taiyu era (AD 472), not Taizong.

proposals.before: When the crown prince's position was fixed, the authorities memorialized, "The crown prince stands second to the throne, and all the realm performs the rites due to officials. Having paid full ritual to the imperial heir, one cannot fail to show respect to his mother. Princesses and noble consorts who may exchange correspondence, and the three ladies of the six palaces who share rank with the honored consort, should all observe toward the honored consort the same rites of respect owed the crown prince. In the Yuanjia era of Song, the retainers of the principalities of Shixing and Wuling all paid official respect to the mothers of their princes, Consorts Pan and Lu. Though the honored consort is not the lesser lord to palace officials, the principle is the same as when in the Taizong reign of Song the hundred officials were ordered to pay official respect to the emperor's mother. Palace staff should show respect in the same manner as officials, presenting memorials of audience at the Divine Beast Gate and offering congratulations at the year's festivals in the same way. Moreover, the crown prince's consort is paired by established grand precedent; for a daughter-in-law to outrank her mother-in-law would further violate proper order. The honored consort's regulations should be entirely the same as the crown prince's."
proposals.after: When the crown prince's position was fixed, the authorities memorialized, "The crown prince stands second to the throne, and all the realm performs the rites due to officials. Having paid full ritual to the imperial heir, one cannot fail to show respect to his mother. Princesses and noble consorts who may exchange correspondence, and the three ladies of the six palaces who share rank with the honored consort, should all observe toward the honored consort the same rites of respect owed the crown prince. In the Yuanjia era of Song, the retainers of the principalities of Shixing and Wuling all paid official respect to the mothers of their princes, Consorts Pan and Lu. Though the honored consort is not the lesser lord to palace officials, the principle is the same as when in the Taiyu reign of Song the hundred officials were ordered to pay official respect to the emperor's mother. Palace staff should show respect in the same manner as officials, presenting memorials of audience at the Divine Beast Gate and offering congratulations at the year's festivals in the same way. Moreover, the crown prince's consort is paired by established grand precedent; for a daughter-in-law to outrank her mother-in-law would further violate proper order. The honored consort's regulations should be entirely the same as the crown prince's."
proposals.reason: Chinese 泰豫 is Taiyu, not Taizong.

proposals.after: Thereupon the honored consort received regulations and ceremonial observances equal to the crown prince's, and in address her words were termed ling (command).
proposals.reason: 言則稱令 means her utterances were classed as ling, not the English title Lady.

proposals.before: In 553, the second year of Chengsheng, they posthumously enfeoffed the empress dowager's adoptive father, the former presentation attendant of Qi Shi Lingbao, as central cavalier attendant and left guard general with the marquisate of Wukang, and her mother Lady Chen as marchioness of Wukang.

proposals.reason: Chinese 父 does not say adoptive, and 齊故奉朝請 modifies Shi Lingbao rather than forming the fused name Qi Shi Lingbao.

proposals.before: In the second year of Chengsheng, they posthumously enfeoffed the empress dowager's father, the former Presentation Attendant of Qi Shi Lingbao, as Central Cavalier Attendant, Left Guard General, and Marquis of Wukang, and her mother Lady Chen as the Marchioness of Wukang.
proposals.after: In the second year of Chengsheng, they posthumously enfeoffed the empress dowager's father, Shi Lingbao, former Presentation Attendant of Qi, as Central Cavalier Attendant, Left Guard General, and Marquis of Wukang, and her mother Lady Chen as the Marchioness of Wukang.
proposals.reason: The phrase of Qi Shi Lingbao fuses the Qi office with the personal name 石靈寶.

proposals.before: As a girl she was gentle and bright; her uncle Wang Jian saw her and said, "She is the instructress of our house."
proposals.after: As a girl she was gentle and bright; her uncle Wang Jian (暕) saw her and said, "She is the instructress of our house."
proposals.reason: The uncle is 暕, a different person from grandfather 儉, but the English repeats the same Wang Jian used for the grandfather.

proposals.before: As a girl the empress was gentle and bright; her uncle Jian saw her and said, "She is the instructress of our house."
proposals.after: As a girl the empress was gentle and bright; her uncle Jian (暕) saw her and said, "She is the instructress of our house."
proposals.reason: Literal Jian collapses uncle 暕 with grandfather 儉.

proposals.before: She bore the lamented crown prince Xiao Daqi, Xiao Dalian, prince of Nankang, and Princess Miaoqie of Changshan.

proposals.before: She bore the Lamented Crown Prince Daqi, Prince Dalian of Nankang, and Princess Miaoqie of Changshan.
proposals.after: She bore the Lamented Crown Prince Daqi, Prince Dalian of Nan commandery, and Princess Miaoqie of Changshan.

proposals.after: That year, when Jianwen took the throne, she was posthumously honored as empress with the posthumous name Jian.

proposals.after: The consort in the twelfth month of the sixteenth year of Tianjian was invested Princess of Xiangdong and bore the Heir Apparent Fangdeng and Princess Hanzhen of Yichang.

proposals.after: The next year her father was posthumously enfeoffed as marquis of Guangde with the posthumous name Wen.

proposals.after: As Chang, Prince Xian of Hengyang, had not yet arrived, they summoned the future Emperor Wen.

proposals.before: In 567, the second year of Guangda, the empress issued an edict deposing the emperor as prince of Linhai and ordering Emperor Xuan to succeed.
proposals.after: In 568, the second year of Guangda, the empress issued an edict deposing the emperor as prince of Linhai and ordering Emperor Xuan to succeed.

proposals.before: That fourth month the ministers proposed the temple name Xuan, and she was buried with her husband at Wan'anling.
proposals.after: That fourth month the ministers proposed the posthumous name Xuan, and she was buried with her husband at Wan'anling.

proposals.after: No member of the empress's family held court office; only an elder clansman of her original Niu clan, Niu Qia, rose to central cavalier attendant.

proposals.before: None of the empress's kin held office at court; only a clansman on her mother's side, Niu Qia, reached Central Cavalier Attendant.
proposals.after: None of the empress's kin held office at court; only an elder clansman of her original clan, Niu Qia, reached Central Cavalier Attendant.

proposals.after: Her father Shen Fashen had been a Liang Anqian central recorder and staff officer.

proposals.after: When Emperor Wu marched against Hou Jing, the future Emperor Wen was in Wuxing; she was captured with him and not freed until Hou Jing fell.

proposals.after: After Emperor Wu took the throne, she became princess of Linchuan.

proposals.before: Her father Fashen was posthumously made grand master of the palace with the golden seal and purple cord, enfeoffed as marquis of Jiancheng with the temple name Gong.
proposals.after: Her father Fashen was posthumously made grand master of the palace with the golden seal and purple cord, enfeoffed as marquis of Jiancheng with the posthumous name Gong.

proposals.after: Her mother Lady Gao was posthumously made lady of Sui'an county with the posthumous name Ding.

proposals.after: They posthumously honored the empress's mother Gao as Lady of Sui'an county, with the posthumous name Ding.
proposals.reason: 綏安縣君 is a county title, and 諡 is a posthumous name.

proposals.before: Shizhi and Zhongju lived inside the palace and decided every matter, while Emperor Xuan remained in the secretariat as governor of Yang with three hundred followers.
proposals.after: Shizhi and Zhongju constantly lived inside the palace and decided every matter, while Emperor Xuan, as governor of Yang, entered the secretariat with three hundred attendants and took up residence there.

proposals.after: At his death he received the posthumous name Cheng.

proposals.after: When he died his posthumous name was Cheng.

proposals.after: In 560, the first year of Tianjia, she became consort of the crown prince.

proposals.before: In the first year of Tianchen she became consort of the crown prince.
proposals.after: In the first year of Tianjia she became consort of the crown prince.

proposals.before: She bore Xiao Jize, heir of Linhai.
proposals.after: She bore Zhize, heir of Linhai.

proposals.before: Empress Liu Xuan of Emperor Xuan of Chen, personal name Jingyan, came from Jie in Hedong.
proposals.after: Empress Liu of Emperor Xuan of Chen, personal name Jingyan, came from Jie in Hedong.

proposals.before: In 563, the second year of Tianchen, they returned to the Chen court and she became princess of Ancheng.
proposals.after: In 561, the second year of Tianjia, they returned to the Chen court and she became princess of Ancheng.
proposals.reason: 天嘉二年 is AD 561; Tianchen is a mistranslation of 天嘉.

proposals.before: In the second year of Tianchen they returned to court with the last ruler; the empress became Princess of Ancheng.
proposals.after: In the second year of Tianjia they returned to court with the last ruler; the empress became Princess of Ancheng.
proposals.reason: 天嘉 is Tianjia, not Tianchen.

proposals.before: When Emperor Xuan died Xiao Shuling, prince of Shixing, raised a rebellion; the last ruler was saved by the empress and an old woman of Wu and thereby escaped harm.
proposals.after: When Emperor Xuan died Shuling, prince of Shixing, raised a rebellion; the last ruler was saved by the empress and an old woman of Wu and thereby escaped harm.
proposals.reason: 始興王叔陵 is Chen Shuling, not Xiao Shuling.

proposals.before: When the last ruler's wounds healed he returned government to her.
proposals.after: When the last ruler's wounds healed, government was returned (he took back the government).
proposals.reason: 歸政 here means returning administration to the emperor, not giving it to the empress.

proposals.before: Her mother was Princess Kuaiji the Reverent, a daughter of Emperor Wu of Liang, who died early.
proposals.after: Her mother was Princess Kuaiji the Reverent, a daughter of Emperor Wu, who died early.
proposals.reason: The Chinese only says 武帝; in this Chen-consort biography she is Emperor Wu of Chen's daughter, not Liang's.

proposals.before: Childless, she adopted the palace woman's son Ziyin as her own.
proposals.after: Childless, she adopted the palace woman Sun's son Ziyin as her own.
proposals.reason: The Chinese names the mother as 孫姬, a palace woman surnamed Sun, which the idiomatic English dropped.

proposals.after: At that time Honored Consort Gong was a lady of the heir apparent; Honored Consort Zhang was ten years old and served her.
proposals.reason: 貴妃年十歲 refers to Zhang Lihua, not Gong; the literal English leaves the honored consort ambiguous.

proposals.after: In 584, the second year of Zhide, they built the Linchun, Jieqi, and Wangxian pavilions before Guangzhao Hall, each tens of zhang high with dozens of rooms.

proposals.before: The beauties Wang and Ji, the fair ladies Zhang and Xue, Ladies Yuan, He, and Jiang, and seven others all shared his favor and took turns on the terraces.
proposals.after: The beauties Wang and Ji, the fair ladies Zhang and Xue, Ladies Yuan, He, and Jiang, seven in all, all shared his favor and took turns on the terraces.
proposals.reason: 等七人 counts these seven named consorts, not seven additional women.

proposals.before: There were also the two beauties Wang and Ji, the two fair ladies Zhang and Xue, Lady Yuan the Bright Deportment, Lady He the Talented Fairness, Lady Jiang the Cultivated Countenance, and seven others — all favored — who in turn sported upon the pavilions.

proposals.before: Under Emperor Xiaowu of Song, Lady Yin's fall and a consort raised to equal the empress brought ruin already extreme.
proposals.after: In the Daming era, Lady Yin's fall, with a consort matching the primary wife, brought ruin already extreme.
proposals.reason: Chinese dates the ruin to the Daming era (大明) and does not name Emperor Xiaowu; the idiomatic English substitutes a ruler name for the reign title.

proposals.before: When Emperor Ming unified the inheritance he corrected emotion into frugal ugliness; the regulations for serving himself were never changed even to clouds.
proposals.after: When Emperor Ming unified the inheritance he forced his feelings into mean frugality; the regulations for serving himself were never changed at all.
proposals.reason: 曾莫雲改 is an intensive never-changed-in-the-least; rendering 雲 as clouds is a fused-word error that obscures the meaning.

proposals.before: Emperor Donghun abandoned the Way, luxury ran wild, and a clever woman toppled the state like Jie and Zhou — the lesson hangs here.
proposals.after: Emperor Donghun abandoned the Way, luxury ran wild, and a clever woman toppled the state — the same sign as Yin and Xia; the lesson hangs here.
proposals.reason: Chinese 同符殷、夏 compares the case to the Yin and Xia houses, not to the personal names Jie and Zhou supplied in the idiomatic English.

proposals.before: Liang Wu meant to be sparing; though Ding Guifei bore the heir and was richly honored, he never made her empress.
proposals.after: Liang Wu meant to be sparing; though the honored consort's splendid beauty was early manifest and she bore the heir and was richly honored, he never made her empress.
proposals.reason: Chinese names only 貴嬪, not Ding Guifei; the idiomatic English invents a personal name not present in this unit.
